description: How SQL injection and XSS work conceptually — and the defensive habits that stop them cold.

screens.body:
Injection happens when attacker input gets treated as commands. Your app meant "store this text" — but the text was secretly instructions, and something obeyed them.

Picture a note that says "Feed the cat. Also, erase the whiteboard." A careful reader feeds the cat and ignores the extra instruction. A careless one erases the whiteboard.

The fix, everywhere: never let data and commands mix. Keep them in separate lanes.

options: Attacker input gets treated as commands
A needle used by hackers
A virus that injects code into your computer
check.question: What is an injection attack, in one sentence?

code.snippet:
// the golden rule of this whole topic:
// DATA (user input) and COMMANDS (SQL, HTML, shell) must never mix.

screens.heading: Injection in one sentence
screens.keyPoint: Data and commands must never mix.

screens.body:
Imagine a login form. Your app builds a database question like: find the user named ___ AND password ___, filling the blanks with what was typed.

If the app glues the typed text straight into that question, a clever input can rewrite the question itself — turning "find this user" into "find every user".

The defense: parameterized queries (placeholders). You send the question with blank slots, and the data separately — the database never confuses the two.

options: Data travels separately from the command, so it can't rewrite it
They make the database run faster
They encrypt the whole database
check.question: How do parameterized queries stop SQL injection?

screens.heading: SQL injection: the concept
screens.keyPoint: Placeholders keep data out of the command.

screens.body:
Cross-site scripting (XSS) is injection aimed at the browser. A user posts a comment — but the "comment" is secretly a script. When others view the page, their browsers run it.

That script runs as your site, so it can read what's on the page or act as the victim.

The defense: escape output. Convert <, >, and quotes into harmless text before showing user content, so the browser displays it instead of running it. Most frameworks do this automatically — don't switch it off.

options: The browser shows the text instead of running it as code
It deletes the user's comment
It blocks the user from the site
check.question: How does escaping stop XSS?

code.snippet: // escaping: dangerous characters become harmless text escapeHtml("hi"); // -> "<b>hi</b>" (displayed, not run)

screens.heading: XSS: the concept
screens.keyPoint: Escape output so browsers display it, never run it.

screens.body:
Validation decides what input is allowed before it ever reaches your code. Think bouncer: name on the list, you get in.

Prefer allowlists over denylists. An allowlist says "usernames are 3–16 letters, digits, underscores" — everything else bounces. A denylist tries to block known-bad inputs and always misses the new ones.

Validate on the server — always. Browser-side checks are nice UX, but attackers skip the browser entirely.

options: You define what's allowed — unknown bad inputs bounce automatically
Allowlists run faster
Denylists are illegal
check.question: Why prefer an allowlist over a denylist?

screens.heading: Validation: the bouncer at the door
screens.keyPoint: Allowlist what you'll accept; validate on the server.

screens.body:
Escaping isn't one-size-fits-all — it depends on where the data lands. HTML-escape for web pages, use placeholders for databases, URL-encode for links.

Same data, different outfit per destination. Encoding for the wrong context is like wearing a raincoat in a pool — technically clothing, totally useless.

Rule of thumb: encode at the moment of output, right where data meets its destination.

options: At the moment of output, for that specific destination
Once, when it first arrives
Only if the user looks suspicious
check.question: When should you encode user data?

screens.heading: Output encoding: dress data for its context
screens.keyPoint: Encode at output, matched to the destination.

screens.body:
Even with escaping, mistakes happen. Content Security Policy (CSP) is a backup lock: a header telling the browser which scripts are allowed to run.

A strict CSP blocks inline scripts entirely — so even if an attacker's script sneaks into your page, the browser refuses to run it.

It's defense in depth for XSS: escaping is the main lock, CSP is the deadbolt. Set it via a response header on your server.

options: Tells the browser which scripts are allowed to run
Encrypts all page content
Blocks users from copying text
check.question: What does a Content Security Policy do?

screens.heading: Content Security Policy: a second lock
screens.keyPoint: CSP is the deadbolt behind escaping's main lock.

screens.body:
Three habits stop nearly all injection attacks:

1. Never build commands by gluing user input in — use placeholders and safe APIs.
2. Validate input with allowlists on the server.
3. Encode output for its destination — and add CSP as backup.

Notice the pattern: check at the door (validation), separate lanes (placeholders), dress for the destination (encoding).

options: Trusting input because it came from your own form
Using placeholders for database queries
Escaping user content before displaying it
check.question: Which habit does NOT help against injection?

screens.heading: The injection playbook
screens.keyPoint: Validate, separate, encode. Every input, every time.

screens.body:
These two OWASP guides are the definitive references — read them before you ship anything that touches a database or renders user content:

• OWASP SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/SQL_Injection_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html
• OWASP XSS Prevention Cheat Sheet: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Cross_Site_Scripting_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html
• OWASP Top 10: https://owasp.org/www-project-top-ten/

screens.keyPoint: These two cheat sheets are the definitive guides — read them before you ship.
